title: Why First-Day-Of-School Accountability Is A Must
author: Michael Linsin
summary: As a direct follow-up to an earlier article laying out three conditions for first-day accountability, Linsin confronts the predictable moment when teachers who fully intended to enforce consequences from hour one instead soften, giving extra warnings or vague promises like 'we'll probably start following our plan on Thursday.' He argues this single moment of weakness — however innocuous it feels on a mostly-harmless first day — is a near-perfect predictor that a teacher won't be consistent for the rest of the year, since it teaches students seven specific lessons about the teacher's unreliability (rules are guidelines, everything is negotiable, there's no urgency). He traces the resulting downward spiral in vivid detail: diminished authority produces more pushback, which produces more teacher stress and irritability, which produces snide comments and raised voices, ending in the same exhausted place as the year before. His counter-argument is that the very first firm follow-through makes every subsequent one easier, building an accumulating 'small, shallow breaths of courage' into the confident teacher a summer of daydreaming imagined.
points: Softening enforcement even once on the first day — extra warnings, vague delays like 'we'll start Thursday' — is a near-perfect predictor of inconsistency for the rest of the year.
Giving in on day one silently teaches students seven specific lessons, including that rules are mere guidelines and everything is negotiable.
Diminished first-day authority produces a predictable spiral: more pushback, more teacher stress, more snide comments and raised voices by year's end.
The reverse is also true — the first firm follow-through makes the next one easier, building momentum toward consistency.
Students at the very start of the year are described as at their most willing and agreeable, wanting discipline and a teacher they can respect — making that first moment especially consequential.
quotes: So . . . are you going to do it? Are you going to start holding students accountable before the big hand gets to the nine (or ten)?
They wobble. They soften. They weaken and then melt for all the class to see.
The hard truth is, this is the moment. You just finished the three conditions. Your students are at their most willing and agreeable.
As soon as you give in to the fear and falsely believe you’re doing your students a favor by waiting and easing into the pool, they learn the following about you: You don’t mean what you say.
Giving in that first time is a near perfect predictor that you won’t be consistent for the rest of the year.
On the other hand, that first firm follow through makes the next one easier. And the one after that easier still.
